Death Reference No. 27 of 2002 
With Criminal Appeal No. 2159 of 2002 and Jail Appeal No. 405 of 2002
lawyer:
Golam Kibria, Deputy Attorney-General with Snigdha Huq, Assistant Attorney-General—For the State-Appellant. 
Probir Neogi with Mohammad Ali Khan, Advocates—For the Condemned Prisoner-Appellant.
parties:
State ------- Appellant
Vs
Md Abdur Rahim Khan ------- Respondent
full_judgment:
21. This is all the evidence adduced by the prosecution on consideration of which the trial Court convicted and sentenced the accused as aforesaid and made this reference for confirmation of the sentence of death. The accused being aggrieved by that judgment and order of conviction and sentence preferred the appeals. 

 22. Mr Probir Neogi, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the concerned prisoner-appellant with Mr Mohammad Ali Khan, Advocate, makes submission supporting the appeal and opposing the reference. He submits that there is no ocular evidence of the occurrence. None of the prosecution witnesses saw the accused to cause death of the deceased. The prosecution sought to connect the accused with the killing on the basis of one circumstance of calling away the deceased by the accused, but that circumstance, according to him, had not been proved upto the hilt. He further submits that it is in the evidence of PW 11 that next night of occurrence at 11-30 PM Mukhlesur Rahman, an uncle of the deceased, accompanying with the local UP Chairman Abdul Bari Howlader went to the police station and informed the police that the dead body of his nephew, who was killed by unknown killer, was recovered from a sugarcane field of one. Abu Sayeed. That information was recorded in the general diary of the police station and on the basis of that GD Entry the police came to the house of the informant with the chairman and another. Thereafter, at about 1-15 AM, the First Information Report Exhibit 1 was recorded. The learned Counsel for the appellant urges that the GD entry made earlier was the first information report wherein it was mentioned that the killer of the deceased was unknown. It was not stated therein that the accused called away the deceased and some time after his dead body was recovered. He submits that the First Information Report Ex 1 is not a First Information Report under section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, but a statement under section 161 of the same Code and, as such, the same is inadmissible in evidence. In this respect he refers the case of Muslimuddin & others vs State reported in 38 DLR (AD) 311. He further submits that it is in the evidence that Bari Chairman, a close relation of the informant, contested in the election with Selim and in that election the accused worked for Selim. It is in the evidence of PW 6 that on the date. of occurrence at about 5-30/5-40 PM Bari Chairman came to the house of the informant and after half an hour he returned to Sirajganj and two hours after he came back with the police. Thereafter, at his instance introducing a new story of calling away the deceased by the accused before the occurrence, First Information Report, Exhibit 1 was lodged. So, according to Mr Neogi, this story of calling away the deceased by the accused before the occurrence is after thought and subsequent embellishment on which no reliance should be placed. Moreover, the story of calling away the deceased by the accused had not been proved beyond reasonable doubt by the evidence on record. The manner of calling away the deceased by the accused given by PW 1 in her deposition is not consistent with the manner given by her in the first information report, Exhibit 1. Furthermore, she did not disclose the fact of calling away the deceased by the accused to the witnesses immediately after the occurrence. PWs 2 and 3 who deposed supporting their witnessing the accused to call away the deceased did not state to the investigating officer that they had so witnessed. Therefore, their evidence in this regard is not acceptable. Mr Neogi further argues that the evidence of PW 10 that the deceased was seen in the company of the accused at 4-00 PM is also not reliable as he was not examined by the investigating officer and none of other PWs corroborated him in this regard. The learned Counsel for the appellant adds that this being a case solely based on circumstantial evidence, proof of motive is 'essential, but no motive has been attributed or proved. PW 1, the mother of the deceased, gave evidence that when her son used to visit their village home he would play with the accused and their relationship was friendly. For that she did not resist when the accused called away the deceased. As regarding requirement of motive in a case like the present one, the learned Counsel for the appellate refers the cases of State vs. Giasuddin and others recorded in 51 DLR (AD) 103 and Sk Shamsur Rahman @ Shamsu vs State reported in 42 DLR (AD) 200. He further submits that the sole circumstance of calling away the deceased by the accused before the occurrence is also not enough to connect the accused with the killing of the deceased. In this respect he refers the case of State vs Khasru @ Syed Mostafa Hossain and another reported in 43 DLR (AD) 182. In the above context he concludes that the prosecution miserably failed to prove the charge leveled against the accused and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of conviction and sentence must be set aside. 

 23. Mr Golam Kibria, the learned Deputy Attorney-General with Ms Snigdha Huq, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the State, makes submission supporting the reference and opposing the appeals. He submits that by the direct evidence of PWs 1-3 it is proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused called away the deceased from their house and some time, after his dead body was recovered from a nearby sugarcane field. PW 10 testified that the deceased was lastly seen in the company of the accused. These proved circumstances that (1) the deceased was called away by the accused from their house and some time after his dead body was found lying in the nearby sugarcane field and (2) the deceased was lastly seen in the company of the accused were incompatible with the innocence of the accused and proved that none but the accused killed the deceased. In this respect the learned Deputy Attorney-General refers the case of State vs Khasru Syed Mostafa Hossain and another reported in 43 DLR (AD) 182 which has also been referred by the learned Counsel for the condemned prisoner-appellant. According to the learned Deputy Attorney-General, the prosecution case having been proved beyond reasonable doubt by the evidence on record there is no ground calling for interference with the impugned judgment and order. 

 24. Undisputedly, the deceased, 10 years old son of informant PW 1, was done to death on the date of occurrence. It is in the medical evidence that his death was due to asphyxia resulting from throttling. PW 13, the doctor who held autopsy of the dead body of the deceased, though in his examination in-chief made a confusing statement inconsistent with his Post Mortem Report, Exhibit 5, that death was due to haemorrhage resulting from three injuries found, he clarified such confusion and inconsistency in cross-examination saying that it was ascertained that the cause of death was due to asphyxia. His such statement given in cross-examination is corroborated by the Post Mortem Report, Exhibit 5, wherein it was stated that death was due to asphyxia resulting from throttling. Thus, it is established that the deceased was done to death and offence of murder punishable under section 302 of the Penal Code was committed. 

 25. Now, the question is the complicity of the condemned prisoner-appellant in commission of such offence. There is no ocular evidence of the occurrence. None of the PWs saw the accused to cause the death of the deceased. So, there is no direct evidence as to the complicity of the condemned prisoner appellant in the killing. The prosecution sought to connect him with the killing of the deceased by the circumstances, (1) that immediately before the occurrence the accused called away the deceased from their house and (2) that the deceased was lastly seen in the company of the accused. Amongst the PWs 1-3 the mother, aunt and cousin of the deceased respectively, said to have witnessed the accused to call away the deceased from their house and PW 10, a cousin of the deceased, said to have lastly seen the deceased in the company of the accused. On the basis of the evidence of those PWs in this regard the trial Court convicted and sentenced the accused. 

 26. Undisputedly, in the afternoon that dead body of the deceased was recovered from a sugarcane field near the house of the informant PW 1 admitted that Abdul Karim, brother of local UP Chairman Abdul Bari Howlader @ Bari Chairman was the husband of her sister-in-law Noor Jahan. Thus admittedly, Bari Chairman was a close relation of the informant. PW 1 further admitted that in the election the members of her father-in-law's family worked hard for Bari Chairman and Alamgir of that family was a devoted worker of the Chairman. It is also in the evidence that in the election the accused worked for the rival candidate of Bari Chairman. The defence case is that at the instance of Bari Chairman with whom the accused had enmity he (accused) was falsely implicated in this case. It is in the evidence of PW 11 that following night of occurrence at 11-30 PM one Mukhlesur Rahman with Bari Chairman went to the police station and informed the police that the dead body of his nephew killed by unknown killer was recovered from a sugarcane field. Entering that information into the general diary of the police station police came to the house of the informant. Thereafter, at 1-15 AM the First Information Report Exhibit 1 was recorded wherein it was stated that before the occurrence at about 4-45 PM the accused called away the deceased from their house and half an hour after his dead body was recovered from a nearby sugarcane field. The information given by Muklesur Rahman to the police station being accompanied by Bari Chairman at 11-30 PM entered in the general diary being earlier one in reality is that First Information Report under section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and the ejahar Exhibit 1 recorded later on is a statement under section 161 of the same Code and, as such, is inadmissible in evidence. In this regard reliance is placed on the case of Muslimuddin & others vs State reported in 38 DLR (AD) 311 wherein it was observed: 

 27. In the instant case, in the earlier information entered in the general diary it was stated the boy was murdered by unknown killer. The accused was not suspected as the killer therein disclosing that the accused called away the deceased before the occurrence. It is in the evidence of PW 6 that at about 5-30/5-45 PM Bari Chairman came to the house of the informant and staying there for half an hour returned to Sirajganj. After two hours he came back with the police. So, it appears that Bari Chairman visiting the house of the informant and knowing everything well went to the police station taking Mokleshur Rahman with him who informed the police that the dead body of his nephew who was killed by unknown killer had been recovered from a sugarcane field. At the tine of giving such information Bari Chairman was with Mokleshur Rahman. In that information given earlier and entered in the general dairy of the police station, it was said that the deceased was done to death by unknown assailant. It was not mentioned that the accused called away the deceased in the First Information Report, Exhibit 1 recorded at 1-15 AM in presence of Bari Chairman. Due to such belated disclosure, the story of calling away the deceased by the accused seems to be an after-thought. It raises serious doubt as to the truth of the story of calling away the deceased by the accused. Moreover, it supports probability of the defence case of false implication of the accused at the instance of the chairman with whom he had strained relationship. 

 28. Now the evidence on record is examined critically for ascertaining the truth of the story of calling away the deceased by the accused before the occurrence. PW 1, in her deposition, stated that on the date of occurrence at 4-00 PM when she was sitting on the stair of their dwelling but with the deceased, her younger son Nishat and PW 3, the accused came there and called away the deceased towards south on the plea of giving him sugarcane. This PW did not depose that she disclosed this fact of calling away the deceased by the accused to anybody. In the First Information Report, Exhibit 1, she stated that on the date of occurrence at about 4-45 PM the deceased went out taking his younger brother (Nishat) on his lap, but some time after he came back and handing over his younger brother to her (informant) again went out. At this the informant coming to the outer house following him (deceased) saw that he was going towards south with the accused. In the FIR it was not stated that when the informant with the deceased, Nishat and PW 3 was sitting on the stair of their dwelling but at about 4-00 PM the accused came there and called away the deceased. The story of calling away the deceased by the accused was totally absent in the FIR. It was said therein that the deceased was seen to accompany the accused towards south. Thus it appears that the evidence given by PW 1 as to calling away the deceased by the accused is inconsistent with her statement in this regard given in the first information report, Exhibit 1. 

 29. PWs 2 and 3 deposed that in their presence the accused called away the deceased from their house, but they did not say so in their statements recorded under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. None of them said to the investigating officer that they witnessed the accused to call away the deceased. Thus, their evidence in this regard being contradictory and inconsistent with their earlier statements made to the investigating officer and not corroborated by any other PW should be left out of consideration. 

 30. PW 10 said that on the date of occurrence at about 4-00 PM on way to the house of his friend he saw the deceased in the house of the accused with the accused to catch bird. But this PW was not examined by the investigating officer and his statement was not recorded under section 161 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. His such non-examination by the investigating officer indicates that he did not disclose to anybody his witnessing the deceased lastly in the company of the accused. Had he disclosed so his statement would have been recorded by the investigating officer. He also did not say that he disclosed such fact to anybody. Moreover, he has not been corroborated by any other PW. So, his evidence of seeing the deceased lastly in the company of the accused is not credible. 

 31. PW 4 is a village headman. The deceased was the son of his sister's son. PW 5 was 80 years old. He was the main village .headman and UP member for twelve years. He was 'Khalu' of the deceased. PWs 4 and 5 consistently said that they did not hear that the deceased was called away by the accused from their house. None said so to them. Nothing could be elicited by the prosecution cross-examining them to discard their credibility. They were not inimical with the informant party but closely related. They had no reason to tell a lie against them. Had any one of PW 1-3 disclosed about calling away of the deceased by the accused why and at whose interest PWs 4 and 5 would suppress it. We find them most competent and reliable witnesses. From their evidence it is found that none of PWs 1-3 disclosed immediately after that the deceased was called away by the accused. Their such credible evidence creates reasonable doubt as to the truth of the story of calling the deceased by the accused before the occurrence. 

 32. PW 6, a brother of the grandfather of the deceased, also did not say that immediately after the occurrence he heard from anyone of PWs 1-3 that the deceased had been called away by the accused before the occurrence. He said to have heard that fact of calling away the deceased by the accused next day of occurrence from the people. PW 7, a village doctor, who immediately after the occurrence on call 'came to the house of the informant and examining the deceased declared him dead, said that he at that time did not hear how the deceased died. Next day in his dispensary he heard from the members of the public that the occurrence took place at the instance of the accused. PW 8 said that PW 1 told him that the accused called away the deceased, and murdered him, but PW 1 did not say that she said so to PW 8. Thus this part of the evidence of PW 8 being hearsay is inadmissible, and not corroborated by PW 1, is unworthy of credit. PW 9, an uncle of the deceased, said that on way back home he heard that an unidentified boy was murdered and on his arrival in his house his wife, daughter and brother's wife (PWs 1-3) disclosing the fact that the deceased was missing requested him to go ahead to search for the boy. At that time they did not say to him that the deceased was called away by the accused. After the dead body was brought in their house PWs 1-3 said to have disclosed to him that the deceased was called away by the accused. But one of PWs 1-3 said that she had said so to PW 9. PW 10 also did not say that any one of the PWs 1-3 disclosed to him that the deceased was called away by the accused. 

 33. On the above reasons we are of the view that the evidence of PWs 1-3 that the accused called away the deceased before the occurrence and that of PW 10 that the deceased was lastly seen in the company of the accused before the occurrence was not trustworthy. Thus the circumstances attributed by the prosecution to connect the accused with the murder of the deceased had not been established. 

 34. Moreover, the circumstances that (1) the accused called away the deceased and (2) that deceased was lastly seen in the company of the accused before the occurrence do not lead us to an inevitable conclusion that none but the accused caused the death of the deceased. In this respect majority judgment of the case of State vs Khasru @ Syed Mostafa Hossain and another reported in 43 DLR (AD) 182 is relied upon. In that case it was proved that the deceased boy was called away by one of the accused and the deceased was found travelling with two accused persons from their village to a distant place by bus and getting down from the bus. In spite of that the accused persons were acquitted as it was not proved that the deceased was seen with the accused persons near the bank of the river where the dead body of the deceased was lying. In the instant case, there is no evidence as to the presence of the accused in the sugarcane field at any time before recovery of the dead body of the deceased therefrom. None saw the accused to go to that sugarcane field or to come out therefrom or be present there at the relevant time. So, in the present case a circumstance leading to an irresistible conclusion as to the complicity of the accused in the killing of the deceased is lacking. 

 35. In a case like the present one based on circumstantial evidence motive plays an important role. In the case of State vs Giasuddin and others reported in 51 DLR (AD) 103 it was held that in a case where there is sufficient direct evidence to prove an offence motive is immaterial and has no vital importance, but when the case is based on circumstantial evidence motive may be a matter for consideration. In the case of Farid Karim vs State reported in 45 DLR 171 it is held that prosecution is not obliged to suggest any motive where there is direct evidence, but in a case which depends on circumstantial evidence motive is an important factor. In the case of Sk Shamsur Rahman @ Shamsu vs State reported in 42 DLR (AD) 200 it is held that in a case based only upon the dying declaration there should have been some evidence of motive, although motive need not be proved in case of direct evidence or as an ingredient of the offence. In the majority judgment of the case of State vs Khasru @ Syed Mostafa Hossain and another reported in 43 DLR (AD) 182, a case based on circumstantial evidence like the present one, motive was searched for. In that case the following observations were made: 

 There is absolutely no material on record to show that anybody, including the parents of the victim boy, had at any stage expressed any suspicion that the respondents might have had any evil motive in calling out and accompanying the victim boy. All that the father (PW 1) said at the trial was that the motive for murder was to give him pain and sorrow for the rest of his life. This is no motive. He did not say why the two young respondents would like to cause him pain and sorrow. Rather it is significant that PW 1 candidly said in cross-examination that as he did not suspect that Khasru would kill Khairul, he did not make any GD entry. The mother (PW 18) said that she did not obstruct her son from going with Khasru. There is no material to suggest even that there might have been some immediate and on the spot reason for the respondents to cause violence to the victim boy or that they were acting at some others behest. Therefore, it seems clear that upon the facts proved and on authority, the two circumstances referred to above are just not and cannot be conclusive evidence as to the guilt of the respondents". 

 36. In the instant case based on circumstantial evidence no motive has been attributed and proved. It is in the evidence of PW 1 that when the deceased would visit village home the accused occasionally would call away him and they would play. Their relationship was friendly. For that PW 1 did not apprehend any evil motive of the accused when he called away the deceased and, as such, she did not resist her son from going with the accused. The above evidence of the mother does not suggest that the accused called away the deceased with the intention to kill him or he had any motive to kill him. So, it is a case without motive. Moreover, the evidence on record does not suggest development of any immediate or on the spot cause of killing the deceased. Thus, in view of the principle of law enunciated in the above cited cases, we are inclined to hold that the circumstances by which the prosecution sought to prove the guilt of the accused are not sufficient for the purpose and are not conclusive evidence of his guilt. 

 37. On the above reasons we are of the view that it has not been proved beyond doubt that the accused caused the death of the deceased or that he had complicity in murder of the deceased. Thus the conviction of the accused is not founded on proper appreciation of evidence. In that view of the matter, we find the accused not guilty. Consequently, his conviction and sentence must be set aside.
